newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Subsidies to swollen fleets threaten fish stocks.
newsitem.headline: Subsidies to swollen fleets threaten fish stocks.

text.p: A leading environmentalist group accused rich fishing states led by the European Union on Monday of plundering the already declining fish stocks of the developing world with their swollen, subsidised fleets.

Fish species are disappearing because of booming demand and fish are being taken from the sea much faster than they can reproduce, but over-fishing by subsidised fleets in distant seas is continuing, the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) said.
At the start of a two-day meeting on the crisis, WWF head Claude Martin urged the world's fishing states to cut the size of their fleets and face up to the worldwide glut in capacity.
"Governments need to agree on a subsidies reform package sooner rather than later," Martin said.

The Swiss-based WWF said 70 percent of the world's commercially important marine fish stocks were fully fished, overexploited, depleted or only recovering, with fish such as haddock, cod, tuna and sharks seen as particularly vulnerable.
But governments continued to prop up the flagging industry with subsidies worth up to $54 billion a year for catches worth just $70 billion annually, the WWF said.

Rich nations are eating more fish -- some 1.79 billion kilos or 3.94 billion pounds were consumed by Americans alone in 1994 -- and their vessels which have overfished their own waters are now plundering fishing grounds of the developing world, it said.
Because of lack of effective surveillance, experts said it was hard to know remaining stock levels and forecast which fish species could be extinct commercially if over-fishing continued.

But they reported continuing destruction of fish populations because of over-fishing especially in Africa, which provides 10 percent of the world catch but where fish may provide up to 60 percent of the animal protein diet.
"African countries have begun to experience for the first time a biological catastrophe that is taking place," said Gareth Porter, a visiting environmentalist from Washington.
"There's been a collapse of the eco-system. Low-value fish species are beginning to take over from high-value fish."

Porter said the European Union, whose many under-used vessels are fishing in distant waters, spent $230 million a year subsidising its fleets in African waters, but African countries received just a tiny fraction of the market value of their fish in licence fees.
The EU is among the world's top five fish importers, led by Japan and the United States.
